coverage_notes:
48 sources after dedup (pool had ~74 entries with 9 URL-level duplicates collapsed). Dedup by URL: PubMed 41343037 (Pelland 2026), SportRxiv /view/460, PubMed 30558493 (Schoenfeld frequency 2019), PMC4961270 (Helms RIR-RPE), PubMed 26049792 (Zourdos RIR-RPE validation), strongerbyscience /volume/, /hypertrophy-range-fact-fiction/, /periodization-data/, and rpstrength volume-landmarks each appeared twice and were merged to one entry. Where merged copies disagreed I reconciled: SBS /volume/ (tagged both T2 and T3) -> T2; Zourdos 26049792 (tagged T1 and T2) -> T1 (it is a validation study, not consensus); SportRxiv #460 -> redistribute-ok (open preprint) while its Springer/PubMed twins stay reference-only as the citation-of-record.

Tiering: T0 = meta-analyses/systematic reviews (volume: Pelland/Schoenfeld-Ogborn-Krieger/Ralston/Baz-Valle; failure: Refalo/Robinson-metareg/Grgic x2; load: Schoenfeld x2/Grgic-fiber/Lopez/Currier; frequency: Schoenfeld-2016/Grgic x3; periodization: Williams/Afonso/Grgic-LP-DUP/Harries; autoregulation/overload: Hickmott/autoreg-NMA-2025/autoreg-review-2021/volume-progression-2024). T1 = RCTs, mostly trained subjects (Schoenfeld 1/3/5-set x2, Schoenfeld IJSPP vol/freq, Robinson iusca, Ruple, Pelland single-set, Refalo failure-RIR, JSSE proximity, Refalo fatigue, Zourdos validation, Plotkin overload, Helms RPE-vs-%1RM, Helms volume-autoreg). T2 = expert consensus/textbook (SBS x7, Henselmans x3, RP x2, MASS, Helms M&S Pyramids, Schoenfeld rep-continuum, Helms RIR-RPE SCJ, Biolayne, Weightology/Krieger). T3 = high-quality practitioner explainers (SBS hypertrophy-range-stats, SBS autoregulation). Weighted to T0/T1 metas+RCTs (33 of 48 are T0/T1) per the brief.

License: redistribute-ok for PMC-OA/CC-BY/CC-BY-NC-ND/.edu-repository/SBS-free-PDF/SportRxiv preprints; reference-only for paywalled journals (Springer/Elsevier/JSS/JSCR/MSSE/Tandfonline/LWW/ResearchGate) and proprietary blogs (SBS live pages, Henselmans, RP, MASS, Weightology, Biolayne); unknown for the Williams PDF on a third-party host (fisiologiadelejercicio). Parser: trafilatura throughout (no GitHub-markdown sources). For paywalled metas with open twins, prefer the open version for extraction and cite the paywalled DOI as canonical (Pelland: SportRxiv #460 over Springer; Robinson proximity: SportRxiv #295 over Springer; Grgic 2018 frequency-strength: vuir PDF + SM-Open over Springer; Schoenfeld rep-continuum: PMC over MDPI).

Named-authorities check vs PLAN.md — all represented: Schoenfeld/Ogborn/Krieger volume (27433992); Baz-Valle volume reviews (8884877, 30063555); Pelland/Nuckols dose-response (460/41343037/Springer + SBS /volume/ + Biolayne); Krieger set-volume (Weightology, Ralston); Refalo/Helms proximity meta-reg (9935748, 295, Springer 2069); Grgic failure-vs-non-failure (9068575, 33555822); Robinson/Pelland effective-reps (iusca/393, SportRxiv 484/295); Schoenfeld/Grgic/Krieger frequency (30558493, 0543-8); Grgic frequency-strength (0872-x, vuir, 6081873); Schoenfeld high-vs-low-load (25530577, JSCR, 7706639); Lopez load NMA (8126497); strength %1RM dose-response (Currier 10579494, Schoenfeld rep-continuum); Williams periodization (0734-y, PDF); Grgic autoregulation/APRE (Hickmott, autoreg-NMA-2025, autoreg-review-2021); Stronger By Science/Nuckols (7 articles); MASS (massresearchreview progression); Helms M&S Pyramids (muscleandstrengthpyramids.com) + Helms RCTs/RIR-RPE; RP/Israetel MEV-MAV-MRV (rpstrength landmarks + rep-range help); Henselmans (3 articles); Zourdos RIR-RPE (26049792, 4961270). PLAN-named RCT examples landed: Schoenfeld 2019 1/3/5 sets (30153194 + VU PDF), RIR/failure RCTs (Robinson iusca, Ruple, Pelland, Refalo), frequency RCT (Schoenfeld IJSPP vol/freq). No named authority dropped.

PLAN coverage by dose axis (all six knobs backed by >=1 T0 + T2 reconciler): volume/weekly_sets (T0 Pelland/Schoenfeld/Ralston/Baz-Valle + T2 SBS/RP-landmarks/Weightology); session_sets/junk-volume tail (RP landmarks, Weightology, Henselmans optimal-volume — disputed upper tail captured for the divergence claim); rep_range/intensity_pct1rm (T0 Schoenfeld-load x2/Lopez/Grgic-fiber/Currier + T2 Schoenfeld rep-continuum/RP/SBS); rir/proximity-to-failure (T0 Refalo/Robinson-metareg/Grgic + T1 Robinson/Ruple/Pelland/Refalo + T2 SBS-RIR/Henselmans/Helms-Zourdos scale — supports the effect-vs-fatigue-cost split via Refalo neuromuscular-fatigue); frequency (T0 Schoenfeld-2016+2019/Grgic x3 + T2 SBS x2); rest_seconds (covered indirectly by Schoenfeld rep-continuum/RP/SBS; no dedicated rest-interval meta in pool — flag as a gap for Phase A reference-chasing if a dedicated rows are needed); periodization/overload/autoregulation/deload (T0 Williams/Afonso/Grgic-LP-DUP/Harries/Hickmott/autoreg-NMA/autoreg-review/volume-progression + T1 Plotkin/Helms x2 + T2 SBS-periodization/DUP/autoregulation, MASS, M&S Pyramids).

Two known gaps to close in a fuller Phase A sweep (neither blocks this registry): (1) no dedicated rest-interval meta (Schoenfeld/Grgic rest-interval 2016 meta would fill rest_seconds rows); (2) no dedicated deload/taper study (only covered narratively via RP landmarks and SBS). These were not in the pooled candidates so are not invented here. Count is 48 — within the requested ~30-50 target and the PLAN's 40-70 sources budget.

sources.title: The Resistance Training Dose-Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain (Pelland, Remmert, Robinson, Hinson, Zourdos) — SportRxiv preprint
sources.notes: Open CC-BY 4.0 preprint of the Pelland/Zourdos volume+frequency dose-response re-analysis (67 studies, 2058 subjects; direct vs indirect fractional set counting). Diminishing returns for both hypertrophy and strength, more pronounced for strength. Use as the fetchable full-text for the paywalled Sports Medicine version. LOAD-BEARING: volume band + frequency equivalence.

sources.title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains — Sports Medicine (Springer)
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed journal version of the Pelland/Zourdos dose-response meta-regression (Sports Medicine 2026; DOI 10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w). Paywalled — canonical citation-of-record; cite via the open SportRxiv #460 preprint.

sources.title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions … Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains (Pelland et al. 2026) — PubMed
sources.notes: PubMed canonical metadata/abstract + DOI/PMID anchor for the Pelland/Zourdos 2026 dose-response meta-regression. Authoritative abstract for the volume re-analysis.

sources.title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: systematic review and meta-analysis (Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger 2017) — PubMed
sources.notes: Foundational Schoenfeld/Ogborn/Krieger hypertrophy volume meta (J Sports Sci 2017; 34 groups/15 studies). Graded dose-response; each added weekly set ~+0.37%; >~9-10 sets/wk larger effect. Paywalled at JSS; PubMed is the canonical abstract. Named authority — volume axis.

sources.title: The Effect of Weekly Set Volume on Strength Gain: A Meta-Analysis (Ralston, Kilgore, Wyatt, Baker 2017) — Sports Medicine, PMC
sources.notes: Weekly-set-volume STRENGTH meta. Graded dose-response; medium/high > low (effect trivial but significant). Open access CC-BY 4.0 on PMC. Anchors the strength-vs-hypertrophy volume split.

sources.title: A Systematic Review of the Effects of Different Resistance Training Volumes on Muscle Hypertrophy (Baz-Valle et al. 2022) — J Human Kinetics, PMC
sources.notes: Baz-Valle 2022 review; the '12-20 weekly sets per muscle group' recommendation for trained men; no meaningful moderate-vs-high difference for quads/biceps. Open access PMC (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0). Named authority — volume axis.

sources.title: Total Number of Sets as a Training Volume Quantification Method for Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review (Baz-Valle, Fontes-Villalba, Santos-Concejero 2018) — PubMed
sources.notes: Baz-Valle 2018 review establishing total-sets-to-(near)failure as a valid volume metric across 6-20+ reps when other variables are held constant. Methodological underpinning for set-counting. PubMed canonical (full text paywalled).

sources.title: How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy? A systematic review and meta-analysis of resistance training frequency (Schoenfeld, Grgic, Krieger 2019) — PubMed
sources.notes: Schoenfeld/Grgic/Krieger frequency-hypertrophy meta (J Sports Sci 2019; DOI 10.1080/02640414.2018.1555906). Frequency does not meaningfully affect hypertrophy when volume is equated. PubMed canonical; full text paywalled. LOAD-BEARING: frequency equivalence. (Two pooled copies merged.)

sources.title: Resistance Training Volume Enhances Muscle Hypertrophy but Not Strength in Trained Men (Schoenfeld, Contreras, Krieger, Grgic et al. 2019) — PubMed
sources.notes: Key trained-subjects RCT: 1 vs 3 vs 5 sets/exercise/session, 8 wk. Hypertrophy favored higher volume; strength similar across groups. MSSE 2019 (paywalled); PubMed canonical abstract. Cited by name in PLAN (Schoenfeld 2019 1/3/5 sets).

sources.title: Resistance Training Volume Enhances Muscle Hypertrophy but Not Strength in Trained Men — accepted-manuscript PDF (Victoria University Research Repository)
sources.notes: Open institutional-repository full-text PDF of the Schoenfeld 1/3/5-set trained-men RCT. Use for full-text method/result extraction where the MSSE version is paywalled.

sources.title: Dose-Response Relationship of Weekly Resistance-Training Volume and Frequency on Muscular Adaptations in Trained Men (Schoenfeld et al. 2019) — IJSPP
sources.notes: Companion trained-men dose-response RCT (Int J Sports Physiol Perform) on weekly volume and frequency. Reinforces graded volume->hypertrophy in trained subjects. Paywalled journal page.

sources.title: Higher volume resistance training enhances whole-body muscle hypertrophy in postmenopausal and older females: a secondary analysis (systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs)
sources.notes: Volume dose-response meta extending the relationship to older/postmenopausal females (higher volume -> greater whole-body hypertrophy). Broadens generalizability beyond young trained men. Paywalled (ScienceDirect/Elsevier).

sources.title: The King of Volume Metas (Biolayne / Layne Norton, REPS) — practitioner breakdown of the Pelland/Zourdos dose-response meta
sources.notes: Expert practitioner commentary contextualizing the Pelland/Zourdos volume+frequency dose-response meta for programming (diminishing returns, direct-vs-indirect sets). T2 interpretation layer; proprietary blog.

sources.title: Influence of Resistance Training Proximity-to-Failure on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis (Refalo et al., Sports Medicine 2023)
sources.notes: Refalo et al. systematic review + meta-analysis: small hypertrophy benefit for training closer to failure. Foundational hypertrophy meta for the proximity angle. CC BY 4.0 on PMC. Named authority — failure axis.

sources.title: Exploring the Dose-Response Relationship Between Estimated RT Proximity to Failure, Strength Gain, and Muscle Hypertrophy: A Series of Meta-Regressions (Robinson/Pelland/Refalo/Jukic/Steele/Zourdos, SportRxiv 2023)
sources.notes: Open-access (CC BY 4.0) preprint of the key meta-regression: continuous RIR modeling shows hypertrophy improves toward failure but flattens ~1-2 RIR; strength insensitive. Open version of the paywalled Sports Medicine 2024 article. LOAD-BEARING: proximity-to-failure.

sources.title: Exploring the Dose-Response Relationship Between Estimated RT Proximity to Failure, Strength Gain, and Muscle Hypertrophy: A Series of Meta-Regressions (Sports Medicine 2024)
sources.notes: Published journal version of the Robinson/Refalo meta-regression (Sports Medicine). Springer landing page (auth-gated full text); cite for canonical DOI. Open-access equivalent is SportRxiv #295.

sources.title: Effects of Resistance Training Performed to Repetition Failure or Non-Failure on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Grgic, Schoenfeld, Orazem, Sabol; J Sport Health Sci 2022)
sources.notes: Grgic failure-vs-non-failure meta: no overall strength/hypertrophy difference; non-failure favored for strength in volume-unequated studies; failure favored hypertrophy in trained subgroup. CC BY-NC-ND on PMC. Named authority — failure axis.

sources.title: Effects of Resistance Training Performed to Failure or Not to Failure on Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy, and Power Output: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis (Grgic et al., J Strength Cond Res 2022)
sources.notes: Second Grgic failure/non-failure meta covering strength, hypertrophy, and power. PubMed record (JSCR full text paywalled); corroborating T0 for the no-meaningful-difference conclusion.

sources.title: The Effect of Resistance Training Proximity to Failure on Muscular Adaptations and Longitudinal Fatigue in Trained Men (Robinson, Helms, Zourdos et al., Int J Strength Cond 2025)
sources.notes: RIR-equated RCT in trained men comparing 4-6, 1-3, 0-3, and 0 RIR: strength comparable 4-6 vs 1-3 RIR, sets to failure slightly inferior; fatigue largely comparable. CC BY 4.0, free PDF. On-angle Zourdos/Robinson RCT.

sources.title: The Effects of Resistance Training to Near Failure on Strength, Hypertrophy, and Motor Unit Adaptations in Previously Trained Adults (Ruple, Plotkin et al., Physiological Reports 2023)
sources.notes: RCT in previously trained adults: low-RIR (0-1) vs high-RIR (4-6); similar strength/hypertrophy plus motor-unit data. CC BY 4.0 on PMC. Key RIR-equated trained-subject RCT.

sources.title: Without Fail: Muscular Adaptations in Single-Set Resistance Training Performed to Failure or with Repetitions-in-Reserve (Pelland/Robinson/Zourdos et al., SportRxiv; pub. MSSE 2025)
sources.notes: Open-access preprint of a trained-subject RCT: single-set FAIL vs 2-RIR, 8 wk; failure modestly enhanced some hypertrophy/power measures but not strength/endurance. Free PDF. Published version paywalled in MSSE 2025.

sources.title: Similar Muscle Hypertrophy Following Eight Weeks of RT to Momentary Muscular Failure or with Repetitions-in-Reserve in Resistance-Trained Individuals (Refalo, Helms, Robinson, Hamilton, Fyfe; J Sports Sci 2024)
sources.notes: Within-subject RCT in 18 resistance-trained adults: leg press/extension to failure vs 1-2 RIR, 8 wk; similar quadriceps hypertrophy. Tandfonline full text 403/paywalled (reference-only); on-angle Refalo RIR-equated trained RCT.

sources.title: Influence of Varying Proximity-to-Failure on Muscular Adaptations and Repetitions-in-Reserve Estimation Accuracy in Resistance-Trained Individuals (J Science in Sport and Exercise 2025)
sources.notes: RCT in resistance-trained individuals varying proximity to failure, plus RIR-estimation accuracy data. Springer landing page auth-gated (paywalled). Adds a recent trained-subject RIR-equated trial.

sources.title: Influence of RT Proximity-to-Failure, Determined by Repetitions-in-Reserve, on Neuromuscular Fatigue in Resistance-Trained Males and Females (Refalo et al., PMC)
sources.notes: Companion study on neuromuscular fatigue across RIR proximities in trained subjects — sources the fatigue-cost half of the failure-cost split claim. PMC open-access (CC BY).

sources.title: Application of the Repetitions in Reserve-Based Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale for Resistance Training (Helms, Cronin, Storey, Zourdos; Strength Cond J 2016)
sources.notes: Foundational practitioner paper defining the RIR-based RPE scale (RPE 10 = 0 RIR) used to operationalize proximity to failure and autoregulation. Helms/Zourdos authors. PMC CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Named authority — measurement/autoregulation context. (Two pooled copies merged.)

sources.title: Novel Resistance Training-Specific Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale Measuring Repetitions in Reserve (Zourdos, Klemp, Dolan, Helms et al., J Strength Cond Res 2016) — PubMed
sources.notes: Original Zourdos/Helms RIR-RPE scale validation (velocity-RPE r=-0.88 experienced / -0.77 novice). Citation backbone for how RIR proximity is measured. PubMed record; JSCR full text paywalled. (Two pooled copies merged; tiered T1 as a validation study.)

sources.title: Training to Failure, or Just Training to Fail? (Stronger By Science / Nuckols team)
sources.notes: Nuckols/SBS expert synthesis of the failure-vs-non-failure and proximity-to-failure literature; practitioner translation of the metas. Proprietary blog (reference-only). Named authority.

sources.title: Overshooting, Undershooting, Or Just Right? How To Perfect Your Ability To Predict Repetitions In Reserve (Stronger By Science)
sources.notes: SBS deep-dive on RIR estimation accuracy (lifters tend to leave more reps than they think) — relevant for interpreting 'estimated' proximity in the meta-regressions. Proprietary blog (403 to fetcher).

sources.title: How Close to Failure Should You Train? (Menno Henselmans)
sources.notes: Henselmans expert-practitioner synthesis: near-failure (a few RIR) matches failure for hypertrophy with less fatigue across ~5-30 reps; practical RIR prescription with an effective-reps mechanistic angle. Proprietary blog. Named authority — failure axis. (Two pooled copies merged.)

sources.title: Muscular adaptations in low- versus high-load resistance training: A meta-analysis (Schoenfeld, Wilson, Lowery, Krieger 2017) — PubMed
sources.notes: Schoenfeld high-vs-low-load meta (Eur J Sport Sci): similar whole-muscle hypertrophy across loads to failure, strength favors heavy loads. Canonical PubMed page; full text paywalled. Named authority — load axis.

sources.title: Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations Between Low- vs. High-Load Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis (Schoenfeld, Grgic, Ogborn, Krieger 2017, JSCR)
sources.notes: Updated, larger high-vs-low-load meta (J Strength Cond Res 2017): hypertrophy similar across loads, 1RM strength greater with heavy load. Publisher full-text page (paywalled).

sources.title: The Effects of Low-Load Vs. High-Load Resistance Training on Muscle Fiber Hypertrophy: A Meta-Analysis (Grgic, Schoenfeld 2020)
sources.notes: Fiber-type-specific load meta on PMC: high-load tends to favor type II, low-load type I; whole-muscle similar. Open access. Nuance for the load angle.

sources.title: Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis (Lopez et al. 2021)
sources.notes: Lopez load network meta (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2021, CC-BY-NC-ND on PMC): hypertrophy load-independent to failure; strength superior with moderate/high load. Core source for the load angle. Named authority.

sources.title: Resistance training prescription for muscle strength and hypertrophy in healthy adults: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis (Currier et al. 2023, BJSM)
sources.notes: Bayesian NMA crossing load x sets x frequency: >80% 1RM maximizes strength; all prescriptions comparable for hypertrophy; higher-load multiset 2-3x/week top-ranked. PMC full text (open). Integrative source across multiple axes.

sources.title: Effects of Resistance Training Frequency on Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger 2016)
sources.notes: Earlier frequency-hypertrophy meta (Sports Medicine 2016): muscles should be trained >=2x/week to maximize growth; non-volume-equated (contrast with the 2019 volume-equated finding). Paywalled journal page. Named authority — frequency axis.

sources.title: Effect of Resistance Training Frequency on Gains in Muscular Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Grgic et al. 2018)
sources.notes: Frequency-strength meta (Sports Medicine 2018): frequency effect on 1RM disappears when volume equated; multi-joint > single-joint. Paywalled; OA PDF mirror at vuir.vu.edu.au. Named authority — frequency axis.

sources.title: Effect of Resistance Training Frequency on Gains in Muscular Strength (Grgic et al. 2018) — Victoria University OA PDF
sources.notes: Open-access institutional-repository full-text PDF of the Grgic 2018 frequency-strength meta. Directly fetchable backup for the paywalled Springer version.

sources.title: Weekly Training Frequency Effects on Strength Gain: A Meta-Analysis (Grgic et al. 2018, Sports Medicine - Open)
sources.notes: Separate frequency-strength meta in Sports Medicine - Open (CC-BY, full text on PMC): ES rises with sessions (0.74->1.08) but no effect when volume equated; multi-joint/upper-body sensitive.

sources.title: Comparison of Periodized and Non-Periodized Resistance Training on Maximal Strength: A Meta-Analysis (Williams et al. 2017, Sports Medicine)
sources.notes: Seminal Williams et al. meta (18 studies): periodized RT superior to non-periodized for 1RM irrespective of volume/training status. Canonical 'Williams periodization meta' cited by name in PLAN. Springer landing page paywalled (abstract free).

sources.title: Comparison of Periodized and Non-Periodized Resistance Training on Maximal Strength: A Meta-Analysis (Williams et al. 2017) — full PDF
sources.notes: Full-text PDF mirror of the Williams 2017 strength meta (third-party host; redistribution rights unclear). Use to read effect sizes (d≈0.43 raw, 0.23 adjusted) since the Springer version is paywalled.

sources.title: A Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses Comparing Periodized and Non-periodized Exercise Programs: Why We Should Go Back to Original Research (Afonso et al. 2019, Frontiers in Physiology)
sources.notes: Umbrella critique of the periodization meta literature (incl. Williams): argues metas conflate periodization with variation and never test predicted adaptation timing. CC-BY 4.0. Key 'limitations of the evidence' source for the periodization claim.

sources.title: Effects of linear and daily undulating periodized resistance training programs on measures of muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Grgic et al. 2017, PeerJ)
sources.notes: 13-study meta finding LP vs DUP equivalent for hypertrophy (d=-0.02); recommends prioritizing volume + progressive overload over periodization-model choice. CC-BY 4.0. Core DUP-vs-linear source (PMC copy preferred over PeerJ landing).

sources.title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Linear and Undulating Periodized Resistance Training Programs on Muscular Strength (Harries, Lubans & Callister 2015)
sources.notes: Strength-outcome counterpart to Grgic's hypertrophy meta: LP vs undulating periodization on strength. Complements the DUP-vs-linear angle. ResearchGate host; underlying journal article paywalled.

sources.title: The Effect of Load and Volume Autoregulation on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Hickmott, Chilibeck, Shaw & Butcher 2022, Sports Medicine - Open)
sources.notes: Meta of load autoregulation (RPE/RIR/APRE) vs standardized loading, plus volume autoregulation via velocity-loss thresholds (~20-25% VL optimal). CC-BY 4.0. Central autoregulation evidence source.

sources.title: Autoregulated resistance training for maximal strength enhancement: A systematic review and network meta-analysis (2025, J Exercise Science & Fitness)
sources.notes: Recent NMA ranking autoregulation methods for 1RM (APRE > RPE > VBRT > percentage-based, SUCRA). PMC open-access. Strongest recent quantitative comparison of autoregulation modalities.

sources.title: Effects of subjective and objective autoregulation methods for intensity and volume on enhancing maximal strength during resistance-training interventions: a systematic review (2021)
sources.notes: Systematic review distinguishing subjective (RPE/RIR) vs objective (velocity-based) autoregulation for intensity and volume; autoregulated groups out-gain percentage/fixed-load groups. PMC open-access. Good taxonomy of autoregulation methods.

sources.title: Progressive overload without progressing load? The effects of load or repetition progression on muscular adaptations (Plotkin et al. 2022, PeerJ)
sources.notes: 8-week RCT in trained subjects: load progression vs rep progression yield near-identical hypertrophy and strength — operationalizes 'progressive overload' beyond adding weight. CC-BY 4.0. Key progressive-overload primary study (load > volume > density is an ordering, not an effect ranking).

sources.title: Progression of total training volume in resistance training studies and its application to skeletal muscle growth (2024, review)
sources.notes: Review/analysis of how total training volume is progressed across RT studies and its relationship to hypertrophy — quantitative framing of progressive overload as volume progression. PubMed record (full text may be paywalled).

sources.title: RPE vs. Percentage 1RM Loading in Periodized Programs Matched for Sets and Repetitions (Helms et al. 2018, Frontiers in Physiology)
sources.notes: RCT comparing RPE-based autoregulated loading vs fixed %1RM in a periodized program; foundational Helms autoregulation study bridging autoregulation + periodization. Frontiers CC-BY.

sources.title: Rating of Perceived Exertion as a Method of Volume Autoregulation Within a Periodized Program (Helms et al. 2018, J Strength Cond Res)
sources.notes: Helms study using RPE to autoregulate VOLUME (not just load) within a periodized powerlifting program. PubMed record; JSCR full text paywalled. Complements the load-autoregulation Helms 2018 paper.

sources.title: Loading Recommendations for Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy, and Local Endurance: A Re-Examination of the Repetition Continuum (Schoenfeld, Grgic, Van Every, Plotkin 2021)
sources.notes: Authoritative narrative review reframing the rep/%1RM continuum: hypertrophy across wide loading zones, strength favors heavy, endurance light. MDPI Sports CC-BY, full text on PMC. Best single rep-range/%1RM guidance source; PMC copy preferred over the MDPI HTML.

sources.title: The Hypertrophy Rep Range — Fact or Fiction? (Stronger By Science, Greg Nuckols)
sources.notes: SBS synthesis: equivalent growth across ~30-85% 1RM when sets are taken near failure, debunking the strict 6-12 'hypertrophy zone'. Key load-selection/rep-range programming source. Proprietary blog. Named authority. (Two pooled copies merged.)

sources.title: The Hypertrophy Rep Range — Stats and Adjustments (Stronger By Science)
sources.notes: Companion SBS piece with the statistical adjustments behind the rep-range conclusion; useful for caveats on load/rep-range hypertrophy equivalence. Proprietary blog.

sources.title: More Training, More Gaining: Everything You Need to Know About Training Volume (Stronger By Science)
sources.notes: Flagship SBS synthesis of the training-volume literature incl. the Pelland/Nuckols dose-response meta they co-authored: weekly-sets dose-response hypertrophy vs strength, diminishing returns, ~4 sets to detect growth up to 30+ fractional sets. Cornerstone volume reference. Named authority. (Pooled duplicates merged; tiered T2.)

sources.title: More Training, More Gaining (free PDF) — Stronger By Science
sources.notes: Official SBS-hosted free PDF of the training-volume article; same content as /volume/ but openly distributed by the publisher, so safe to cache/redistribute. Archival copy of the volume synthesis.

sources.title: Training Frequency for Muscle Growth: What the Data Say (Stronger By Science)
sources.notes: SBS meta-analytic synthesis of training frequency for hypertrophy (13 studies, 305 subjects): frequency mostly matters as a vehicle for weekly volume; per-set equivalence when volume matched. Core frequency-for-size reference. Named authority.

sources.title: Training Frequency for Strength Development: What the Data Say (Stronger By Science)
sources.notes: Companion SBS synthesis on training frequency for strength gains; frequency effect on 1RM and interaction with volume. Pairs with the hypertrophy-frequency article for complete frequency programming guidance.

sources.title: Periodization: What the Data Say (Greg Nuckols, Stronger By Science)
sources.notes: Nuckols' evidence review (~51 studies coded): periodized > non-periodized for strength; undulating > linear for trained (not untrained) lifters; effects stronger for bench than squat. Authoritative practitioner synthesis of the periodization angle. Proprietary blog. Named authority. (Two pooled copies merged.)

sources.title: Daily Undulating Periodization: The Bogeyman of Training Programs (Stronger By Science)
sources.notes: SBS deep-dive on DUP — theory (repeated-bout effect / stimulus variation) and evidence for varying sets/reps/loads per session. Complements the periodization overview for practical program structuring.

sources.title: The Science of Autoregulation (Stronger By Science)
sources.notes: High-quality practitioner explainer on autoregulation concepts (RPE/RIR, readiness-based load/volume adjustment) tying together autoregulation research for applied programming. Proprietary blog.

sources.title: Closer to Failure, Bigger Muscles: What Science Says About RIR (Stronger By Science)
sources.notes: 2025 SBS synthesis of proximity-to-failure/RIR research (incl. Robinson et al. 2023 meta-regression): lower RIR -> more hypertrophy, near-flat for strength, comparable across ~0-4 RIR. Primary RIR/effort-prescription reconciler. Named authority.

sources.title: New science on the optimal training volume: extreme training for extreme gains? (Menno Henselmans)
sources.notes: Henselmans synthesis arguing trained lifters may benefit from higher weekly volumes (up to ~45 sets) than the conventional 10-20; covers recovery/individual response and the volume-frequency interaction. Counterpoint/extension to the SBS volume view; surfaces a disputed upper-tail. Named authority.

sources.title: Optimal program design 2.0 (Menno Henselmans)
sources.notes: Henselmans integrated program-design framework synthesizing volume, frequency, intensity, exercise selection and split structure into practical recommendations. One-stop programming-synthesis source. Named authority.

sources.title: Program your sets like this for faster gains (autoregulation & progression) (Menno Henselmans)
sources.notes: Henselmans on autoregulation and load/rep progression — argues autoregulated progression outpaces fixed weight x rep schemes. Core progression/autoregulation programming reference. Named authority.

sources.title: Set Volume for Muscle Size: The Ultimate Evidence Based Bible — Weightology (James Krieger)
sources.notes: James Krieger's comprehensive set-volume guide building on his meta-analyses (logarithmic per-session dose-response, multi- vs single-set, weekly-volume diminishing returns ~>20 sets). Authoritative volume synthesis; partially paywalled members area. Named authority (Krieger set-volume meta).

sources.title: Training Volume Landmarks for Muscle Growth (Renaissance Periodization / Israetel)
sources.notes: RP/Israetel's canonical article defining MV/MEV/MAV/MRV volume landmarks with progression and deload logic — the min/max/recommended scaffolding for weekly_sets rows (graded against the T0 metas). Freely readable but proprietary (promotes paid apps). Named authority — volume landmarks. (Two pooled copies merged.)

sources.title: What should my rep range be? (Renaissance Periodization / Israetel)
sources.notes: RP practical rep-range guidance: ~5-30 reps effective for hypertrophy if near failure, with compound vs isolation %1RM nuance. T2 expert-consensus practitioner reference for rep_range/intensity rows.

sources.title: A Progression Framework for Hypertrophy — MASS Research Review (Eric Helms)
sources.notes: Eric Helms (MASS Vol.4 Iss.7) practical framework for progressing hypertrophy training (load/rep/volume progression decisions). Public preview; full text paywalled. Authoritative MASS progression reference. Named authority — MASS reconciler.

sources.title: The Muscle and Strength Pyramids (Nutrition & Training) — Eric Helms et al.
sources.notes: Official site for Helms' Muscle & Strength Training Pyramid (2nd ed.) — the hierarchy-of-importance programming model (adherence > volume/intensity/frequency > progression > exercise selection > rest > tempo), mapping ~1:1 onto the overload hierarchy this leaf encodes. Foundational evidence-based programming textbook; book is proprietary. Named authority.
